posts.content_md:
Hey, I haven't posted here in ages because I've not been able to ever get my laser system up and running, but I had an interesting thought and I was curious if anyone here might be interested in doing a collaboration.

I design super high end LED light fixtures ([http://web.mit.edu/neltnerb/www/artwork/](http://web.mit.edu/neltnerb/www/artwork/)) that I use to illuminate paintings to very cool effect. It occurs to me that it might look absolutely awesome to illuminate a multichromatic hologram with my lights! I don't have a very good idea of what might happen, but I think it would be a very neat visual experience.

If someone would be willing to make me tiny test holograms made with multiple laser frequencies, I would love to see how they work. If they turn out to be awesome, I would be thrilled to provide free LED lighting for your exhibit in exchange for holograms for mine. Further if you were interested, I could even try to sell them here as a unit and split the proceeds =) My suspicion is that LED lights with holograms may well be far, far cooler together than either would be apart!

I live in Boston, MA.

Cheers,

Brian Neltner

[neltnerb@mit.edu](mailto:neltnerb@mit.edu)

posts.content_md:
The metre square stereogram transmission holograms I made at HoloNorth can be illuminated with LED's. See John Perry's website where he shows my holograms (David Warren) lit with amber LED's. In fact I have lit them with numerous different coloured LED's and they are pin sharp (each colour does require a change in the angle of reconstruction to suit the wavelength). At present they are lit with a metal halide light at an exhibition because the gallery is essentially a glass box outside and the holograms have to compete with the sunlight. There is a slight sacrifice in sharpness, but not too much. They were made at Holonorth to be lit with LED's similar to the portrait made by John of the Queen. 

zipsister

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Idea: LED light illuminated Holograms. Anyone want to try?
posts.content_md:
meekan01, yes the base pattern or image would be displaced by the angle difference in the LED's. 

What's more, one could use full color film and have different pattern colors at different depths. In other words, we could have a blue shape or pattern at 2 inches behind the plate and one 2 inches in front of the plate. Then we could have a green pattern at 1 inch in front and a red pattern one inch behind. Our array of LED's would be of all three colors. This would give the effect that you some patterns are in front of or in back of the other patterns and as you moved side to side, the paralax would surely show. We could also get more creative and use 2 LED's for each color, providing a double image for each pattern. If the separation of the two same colored lights is enough, the two images of the same pattern would be separated enough to look like two patterns. Then if we throw in a white, broad band pattern, we would get a single colored image from each of the LED's displaced by the difference in separation of the LED's.

Most raw LED's (no diffuser or collimator) do very well as a point source illuminator for holography. In fact, because they are so narrow band, they provide very crisp detail.

In my opinion, using multiple LED's, even as far as multiple colored LED's would sure open this medium up for the creativity of an artist. Right now I am picturing abstract shapes and colors at different depths. Some shapes are flat and some are 3D but the different depths would produce some very interesting paralax.

I imagine the pattern would look translucent and not opaque in the hologram where they overlap.

posts.content_md:
Hi John!

That's absolutely marvelous, you did nearly the exact same experiment with your pigments as I did; I even had them laid out similarly on a posterboard for illumination =) I absolutely love the idea of moving the LEDs around, and I don't think it would be too hard to motorize an array.

I don't really know much about lasers, but...

my lights have the ability to put out true 626, 617, 590, 530, 505, 470, and 455 nm light in arbitrary relative brightnesses, and I can throw in 385nm UV as well (can people make blacklight holograms?).

this is *somewhat* useful in conjunction with painting, and it allows me to address individually well-chosen pigments in the same way you're talking about addressing individual images. however, pigments seem to inevitably have multiple reflection peaks, so I haven't found any that strongly reflect at, say, 505nm but not 530nm. 

but with holograms, where the frequency information contained in the image is so precisely determined by the frequency of the laser light, you could encode nearly delta function reflectances! You could literally encode seven images, one at each frequency, at all sorts of different depths and grid spacings! That sounds super sweet.

And the idea of a blacklight hologram -- this was probably impossible to illuminate previously, because only very recently have UV LEDs been bright enough to do anything. The ones I'm using now cost almost $60 a piece, but they are nearly as bright per LED as a small blacklight fluorescent bulb (~330mW). I'm usually a bit worried about using the UV LEDs without a diffuser over them because a strong point source of UV is damaging to the eyes, but they *are* point sources of UV light. If the viewer was adequately protected by other means, it should work quite well to illuminate a hologram.

I need to redo some of my tests on pigments (made the silly mistake of painting on white board, so it's hard to tell which is actually reflecting more... the color with the least contrast was usually the best reflector), but then I should be posting those results on my website soon if you want those too. They're mostly golden (brand) acrylic paints, as well as a number of fluorescent paints that I wanted to look at because of the UV LEDs in my fixture.

posts.content_md:
Hey meekan01, I too found it quite difficult to find paints that have a very narrow and single line of reflectance. Shortly after I posted my finding on the forum someone suggested a book that had the spectral reflectivity of different pigments in it. I think it was Artist's Handbook or Painters Handbook or something. I reviewed the spectral charts of pigments and found most have a peak that goes down at other wavelengths but rarely goes to 0. Some have two peaks. If your interested in the book, I will pull it off the shelf and post the name and author. It surely is a great resource to have.

I pondered for weeks trying to figure out how to make a glow in the dark hologram. The trick is, we can make a UV hologram but the viewer will not see a UV image. The blacklight effect uses Fluorescent paints. These absorb UV but reflect another color in the visible range. So with a glow in the dark hologram we have to somehow convert the UV image wavefront off the hologram to a visible wavelength and use some Fluorescent technique to get those really pastel reds and greens.

posts.content_md:
Hi Solarenemy,

I've got a lot of experience with LED lighting; my conclusion after working with them extensively is that they're big advantages really shine when you want colored light -- they're less efficient, not as bright, etc, etc as CFLs otherwise. Basically, with a white light, to get green illumination you remove photons whereas with an LED you start with blue photons and then take them away to make white.

Anyway, you probably know all of that, but I wanted to suggest that you may get much better light output by using colored LEDs (not color-changing, but monochromatic) at the frequencies you're interested. If you're making a red hologram, you can use one of the Philips Lumiled Red Rebels and they will give you 85 lumens at only 2.1W (700mA, ~3V). On the other hand, if you use a white LED, only a small amount of the light emitted is red, so even though they put out as much as 180 lumens at 2.8W (700mA, ~4V), the light that will actually be in the range you want is only a small fraction of the total (probably less than 10% from the graphs I'm looking at).

So, if you wanted to, you could replace the white LED in your flashlight with a colored one and probably make your usable illumination increase by ~4-5 times with no additional power usage.
